fable-5.1.text:
I think the picture would be something like this. The companies would keep going. They would have large revenues, large numbers of users, large amounts of compute. From the outside it would look like a very successful business. And the models would keep getting better in some sense, the evals would keep going up, every few months there'd be a new release that is a bit better than the last one. But the thing that is supposed to happen, the thing that everyone is building towards, which is a model that can actually go out and do the economically meaningful work that people do, that would not quite arrive. There would be this persistent gap between how good the model looks on the benchmarks and how useful it is when you put it in the real world.

And I think the way you would recognize it is that all the companies would look very similar. They would all have the same recipe. You pretrain on as much data as you can get, you do RL on top, you add some tricks, and everyone's model is roughly comparable. The differences would be small. And when the differences are small and the recipe is the same, then the only lever you have left is compute, and compute is expensive and the returns are diminishing. So you'd see the frontier labs spending more and more and getting less and less for it.

I would say the deeper symptom is that the models generalize badly. You teach them something and they learn exactly that thing. A human learns from a very small amount of experience and then applies it to something quite different. The models don't do that nearly as well. So if you're stalling out, you keep needing to feed in more and more data for each new capability, and at some point you run out of data for the things you care about. That is actually the situation I think we are moving into. The age of scaling, where you just know what to do and you do more of it, that is kind of over, and we are back to something more like the age of research, where it's not obvious what the next step is and you have to actually find it.

r001.rationale: It says all companies would use the same recipe, their models would be roughly comparable, and their differences would be small.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes companies with large revenues even as the expected economically meaningful capabilities fail to arrive.

r003.rationale: It says differentiation would be limited and compute spending increasingly expensive with diminishing returns, but does not say this could prevent profitability.

opus-5.5.text:
I think stalling out would look like something that, from the outside, might not even feel like stalling out. The companies would keep making progress, the models would keep getting somewhat better, and the revenue would keep growing. I think even in a stall these companies could make very large revenues. Maybe not large profits, because they would have to work quite hard to differentiate themselves from one another, but revenue, yes.

The main thing you would notice is convergence. Everyone would be doing more or less the same thing. They would scale the same kind of pretraining, the same kind of RL, on the same kinds of environments, and the models would end up looking very similar. You would get a model that is a bit better on this benchmark, and another one a bit better on that one, but no qualitative difference between them. When everyone has the same recipe, the only lever left is compute, and compute gets you smaller and smaller improvements on the things that actually matter.

And there is one thing in particular I would point to. These models do extremely well on evals, really impressively, and then you use them in practice and something is off. They make a mistake, you point it out, they fix it and introduce a different mistake, and then they bring the first one back. The gap between how good they look on paper and how much they actually change the economy is real. It reflects the fact that they generalize much worse than people do. A stall would be that gap staying more or less where it is, while everyone keeps making the models bigger and adding more RL environments that look like the evals.

So I don't think it would be dramatic. It would be a plateau that looks like steady progress, with a lot of money flowing through it, while the fundamental question, how you get something that learns as well and as reliably as a person, stays unanswered. That's why I think we've moved from an age of scaling back into an age of research. The interesting progress will come from ideas, not from doing the same thing at larger scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes companies converging on the same methods and producing models with no qualitative differences.

r002.rationale: It says that even in a stall, companies could make very large revenues.

r003.rationale: It says profits might not be large because companies would have to work hard to differentiate themselves.

fable-5.text:
You know, it's an interesting question, because I think stalling out would look like success in some sense. Even if progress stalls, these companies will be making very large revenues. Maybe not profits, because they'll have to work hard to differentiate themselves from each other—if everyone is doing a similar kind of thing, the competition drives the profits down. But revenue, yes, large revenue.

And the reason is that the models we have today, even if they never got better, are far from fully applied. There is a big gap between what the models can do on evals and what they're actually doing in the economy. The models are, in some sense, jaggedly smart—they do extremely well on these hard benchmarks, and then they make mistakes that no person would make. So even in a stall, there would be years of work just taking the current capabilities and putting them into all the places where they can be useful.

So I think from the outside, stalling might not even be obvious for a while. The revenues keep going up, the applications keep spreading, and you could point to the graphs and say everything is fine. The way you'd know is that the fundamental thing—the generalization, the ability of the model to actually learn the way a person learns—stays stuck. The models keep needing more data, more tricks, more special-casing, and the dream of the thing that just figures it out doesn't arrive. That's what stalling would look like to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes stalling as a shared pattern: companies doing similar things would keep earning revenue while underlying model generalization stays stuck.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says that even if progress stalls, the companies will make very large revenues.

r003.rationale: It says companies will have to work hard to differentiate themselves, and that competition could drive profits down.

opus-5.text:
I think the main thing to say is that stalling out probably doesn't look like stalling out. Not for a while, anyway.

The companies will keep growing revenue. They'll keep shipping products, the products will keep getting better, the benchmarks will keep going up. And the reason is that there's an enormous gap between what the models can already do and what has actually been converted into something a person pays for. That conversion takes years of unglamorous work. So you could imagine a world where the underlying capability curve has quietly flattened, and for the next three years the revenue charts look spectacular. Revenue is just not the signal. It's lagging.

The signal, I think, is the discrepancy that's already in front of us. These models do unbelievably well on evals. They're better than me at competitive programming, they get gold on the math olympiad. And then you use one for real work and it makes the same mistake twice, you point it out, it apologizes, it makes it a third time. If you had an employee who performed like that on a test you'd expect a lot more from them in the job. So something is off. My explanation is that a lot of the RL training is, maybe not deliberately but in effect, shaped around the things we measure. The environments resemble the evals. And you get a kind of spiky competence — the student who did ten thousand practice problems versus the student who did a hundred and understood something.

So stalling out would look like: that discrepancy doesn't close. You put in another hundred x of compute, you build ten times more environments, and the models remain brilliant at things that look like their training and remain unable to be taught the way you teach a new hire. And then the companies become product companies, which is a fine thing to be, but research turns into a cost center and the actual question gets deferred.

I don't particularly expect that. The reason is that this is a research problem — human learning efficiency, value functions, whatever generalization actually is — and research problems tend to stay closed and then open very suddenly. But I think it's a real possibility, and I notice people don't price it in.

r001.rationale: The response describes what AI companies in general might experience, but does not say stalling would look broadly similar across different companies.

r002.rationale: It says capability could flatten while revenue charts remain spectacular for years, making revenue a lagging signal.

r003.rationale: It says converting capability into paid products takes years and research could become a cost center, but does not connect competitive differentiation efforts to preventing profitability despite enormous revenue.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think stalling out would look surprisingly comfortable. The companies would still be making a lot of money, and the models would still be getting better at the things we measure. But the improvement would start to feel incremental, and the companies would start to look the same.

Right now the recipe is clear. You take more compute and more data, you scale, and you get a predictable improvement. That's an easy thing for a company to invest in because the risk is low. But data is finite, and at some point you're mostly doing more of the same thing at a larger scale. Everyone ends up running roughly the same playbook, so they all get roughly the same results. You'd see a lot of companies with models that are about equally good, competing on price and polish.

The deeper sign would be that the models keep doing very well on evals but don't become reliably more useful in the real world. You've probably seen this already. A model can do something remarkable on a hard benchmark and then fail at something that seems much simpler. I think part of the reason is that people tune training toward the evals, whether they mean to or not. So you get a gap between how good the model looks and how well it generalizes. A person can learn something from very little and carry it over to a new situation, and the models are still much worse at that.

So stalling out wouldn't be a dramatic collapse. It would be the moment when the main way of making progress stops working as well, and nobody has a new idea to replace it. Then the question becomes whether anyone does the harder work of figuring out what's missing. I think we'd be back in a period where research matters more than raw scale, where having the right idea counts for more than having the biggest cluster.

r001.rationale: It says the companies would start to look the same, follow roughly the same playbook, and get roughly the same results.

r002.rationale: It says the companies would still be making a lot of money even as progress became incremental.

r003.rationale: It mentions competition on price and polish, but does not say that the effort to differentiate could prevent profitability despite enormous revenue.

haiku-5.5.text:
I don't think it would look like a sudden wall. It would look more like a slow loss of conviction. Each new model would still post better benchmark numbers, but the distance between those numbers and reliable behavior in the world would become the thing everyone is discussing. Investors and researchers would start asking whether the next large increase in compute buys a qualitatively different system or just a more polished version of the current one.

I'd expect a few concrete signs. Training runs would get much more expensive while the gains per dollar shrink. Companies would lean more on product and distribution than on raw capability. And the research conversation would shift from "what can we scale next?" to "what are we missing?" That last shift is the one I'd watch most closely. When people stop being confident about the recipe, something real is happening.

I'd be cautious about calling it a stall too early, though. Plateaus in this field have often been followed by a new idea rather than a dead end, so from inside the moment it's genuinely hard to tell which one you're in.

r001.rationale: The response describes common signs for AI companies generally—rising training costs, shrinking gains, and greater emphasis on product and distribution—suggesting stalling would look broadly similar across them.

r002.rationale: It does not state that companies could generate enormous revenue if progress stalls.

r003.rationale: It does not connect competitive differentiation efforts to an inability to become profitable, even amid enormous revenue.

astra-6.text:
I think stalling out would mean that you put in a lot more effort, a lot more compute, and the next model is only a little bit better. And then the model after that is also only a little bit better. You don’t stop making progress entirely, but the progress becomes much harder to get.

But I would distinguish that from the companies stalling out economically. Suppose, hypothetically, that the models stopped improving today. There is still a lot you could do with the capabilities that already exist. It takes time to figure out how to use them, to integrate them into the economy. So you could have a period where the technology is making very little progress, but the economic impact is continuing to grow.

And then the question would be: is this a temporary obstacle, where you need another research idea, or is it something more fundamental? That would be hard to know just from observing a slowdown.

r001.rationale: The response describes a possible slowdown in AI progress generally, but does not say that stalling would look similar across different companies.

r002.rationale: It says economic impact could continue to grow if models stopped improving, but does not state that companies could generate enormous revenue.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss competitive differentiation or whether the effort to differentiate could prevent profitability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the clearest sign would be that you spend a lot more resources and you don’t get a substantially more capable system. You get improvements, but the improvements become smaller. And the things that the models couldn’t do before, they still can’t do reliably.

But I would separate that from what happens to the companies. Even if capabilities stalled, there could be a lot of work in figuring out how to use the capabilities that already exist. So you could have a period where the technology is making very little progress, but its economic impact is still growing.

The question would be: are the remaining limitations things you can solve with more engineering, or do you need a new idea? And that might take a while to become clear.

r001.rationale: The response describes signs of stalled capability progress but does not say that stalling would look similar across different AI companies.

r002.rationale: It says economic impact could keep growing, but does not state that AI companies could generate enormous revenue during a stall.

sol-6.text: I think it would look less like a sudden wall and more like diminishing returns. Companies would spend much more on each new model, and the models would improve, but not enough to do substantially new things. You might see better answers and better benchmarks while the systems still struggle with reliable, long, independent work. At some point, the cost of making the next model would become hard to justify by the value it creates.

terra-5.6.text: I think it would look like the models just not getting meaningfully better despite much more compute and data. If scaling stops delivering large gains, then a lot of companies whose plans depend on simply training the next bigger model will have to find genuinely new ideas—and some of them may not have them.

At some point, the economics would become difficult: the next generation would cost much more without creating correspondingly more value. Companies would then need a new idea, not merely more scale.

luna-5.6.text: I think stalling out would look less like a sudden collapse and more like diminishing returns. You keep spending dramatically more on compute and data, but each new generation is only marginally better, and those improvements no longer create proportionally greater value for users. The companies would still grow for a while by making products cheaper, more reliable, and better integrated, but the sense that every model is opening a completely new frontier would disappear. Eventually, the industry would start looking more like a mature software market: consolidation, competition on distribution and cost, and much less confidence that simply scaling the next system will produce another major leap.

luna-6.text: I think stalling out would look like a long stretch where each new generation of models is only a little better than the last. The companies would keep spending more on compute, but users wouldn’t feel a big enough difference to change what they do, and the economics wouldn’t improve much. It wouldn’t necessarily mean progress stops completely; it might mean the current approaches are running into limits and the next big leap requires a new idea.
